name: A La Baguette
description:
A small French bakery at 74 Rue Lavaud, and you can usually smell it before you see it. Baguettes come warm from the oven, alongside croissants and raisin bread, and the almond croissant is the one visitors talk about. It is a walk-up counter rather than a café.

It only opens Wednesday to Sunday, and closes at midday.
Local tip: Get there close to the 7.30am opening. The cabinet empties fast, and by late morning the best of it is gone.
hoursNote: Closed Mon and Tue; Wed to Sun 7.30am to noon; sells out early

name: Akaroa Harbour Nature Cruise
description:
A two hour Black Cat cruise out of Akaroa to look for Hector's dolphins, the world's smallest dolphin, along with fur seals, white-flippered penguins and seabirds beneath the harbour's volcanic cliffs. Adults are $130, children 5 to 15 are $60, and under 5s go free.

The dolphins live in the harbour all year. If you don't see any, you get a voucher for another cruise rather than a refund.
Local tip: Check in at 61 Beach Road, not the Main Wharf, which is closed for redevelopment, and be there 20 minutes before departure.
hoursNote: Daily at 10.45am and 1.30pm, plus 3.45pm Dec to Mar; check in at 61 Beach Road 20 min before

name: The Common Cafe & Garden Bar
description:
A café and garden bar a little away from the busiest part of the village, with good coffee, a modern brunch menu and generous plates. There is plenty of garden seating, and dogs are welcome at the outdoor tables.

It is a favourite for starting the day, which means on busy mornings the wait for coffee and food can stretch to 20 to 40 minutes.
Local tip: Don't come in a hurry. Order, then browse the bookshop and the local wares shop in the same courtyard while you wait.
hoursNote: Mon to Wed 8.30am to 3pm; Thu to Sun 8.30am to 8pm; evening bookings recommended

name: Barrys Bay Cheese
description:
A traditional cheese factory and shop at Barrys Bay, on the main road on the way into Akaroa. Tasting the range is free, a window looks into the factory, and a shelf of cheaper misshapen "oddities" is worth a rummage.

Cheese isn't made every day, so you may not see production, but the shop and tasting are open daily. A coffee cart is often parked outside.
Local tip: Stop on the way home rather than on the way in, so your cheese isn't sitting in a hot car all day.
hoursNote: Shop open daily 9am to 5pm; closed 25 Dec; factory production not every day

name: The Giant's House
description:
Artist Josie Martin's mosaic garden on the hill above Akaroa, built around a historic house and filled with tiled sculptures, figures and terraces that tumble down through the flower beds. Nothing else in Akaroa looks like it. Adults are $35 and children 2 to 15 are $20, with family passes available.

There is a café and a gallery on site. It is a short but steep walk up Rue Balguerie from the waterfront.
Local tip: Allow at least an hour, since the fun is in the detail, and note it closes earlier, at 3pm, from May to September.
hoursNote: Oct to Apr 11am to 4pm; May to Sep 11am to 3pm; last entry 20 min before close; closed 25 Dec

name: Akaroa Museum
description:
A small, free museum on Rue Lavaud telling Akaroa's story: Ngāi Tahu, the French settlers of 1840, whaling and the British. Your visit also takes in the historic courthouse and the Langlois-Eteveneaux cottage next door.

It is well laid out and bigger than it looks, and a looping video gives a good overview of the whole peninsula. Most people stay longer than they planned.
Local tip: Come here first, before wandering the village. The French street names and old buildings make far more sense afterwards.
hoursNote: Daily 10.30am to 4pm (to 4.30pm Oct to Apr); closed 25 Dec and Anzac Day morning; free entry

name: Diamond Harbour Ferry and Coastal Walk
description:
An easy, cheap half day out. The public ferry from B Jetty in Lyttelton crosses the harbour to Diamond Harbour in 8 to 10 minutes, and from the wharf a clifftop coastal track follows the edge of the bay, with views back to Lyttelton and out towards the heads.

Ferries run often through the day, you pay on board, and there is no need to book. Diamond Harbour has a couple of small cafés, and there are toilets a short walk up the hill from the wharf.
Local tip: Reach B Jetty over the pedestrian overbridge from Lyttelton township, and on busy summer weekends catch a mid-morning sailing, since the middle of the day fills up.
hoursNote: Ferry runs daily from early morning to evening; about 8 to 10 minutes each way; pay on board, no bookings; departs B Jetty, Lyttelton

name: Pōhatu Penguins
description:
Evening tours to watch little penguins (kororā) come ashore at Pōhatu Flea Bay, a conservation project on a working farm on the far side of Banks Peninsula. A 4WD minibus takes you from Akaroa over the back-country roads, and the guides lead you to the nesting boxes with binoculars and camouflage gear to watch the birds return from the sea. Adults are $95 and children 5 to 15 are $55.

Spring and early summer are best, with adults nesting and chicks from October. In winter your chances are roughly 50/50. Reviewers rave about the guides.
Local tip: Tour times move with the sunset, so confirm yours when you book, bring a warm layer for the evening, and keep the flash off.
hoursNote: Evening tours; departure time varies with daylight; about 3 hours; best Sep to Dec and Apr to May; no flash photography

name: Okains Bay Māori and Colonial Museum
description:
A far bigger museum than you would expect in a tiny bay on the outer peninsula, with nationally significant taonga Māori and early colonial collections spread through a cluster of heritage buildings. Highlights include carved waka, hei tiki, wakahuia treasure boxes, pounamu, scrimshaw and huia beak brooches.

Adults are $15, children under 13 go free with an adult, and concessions are $10. It is about 25 minutes from Akaroa over the Summit Road, and reviewers say two or three hours goes quickly here.
Local tip: It is closed on Tuesdays and Wednesdays, so plan your outer bays day around that, then walk down to the beach afterwards.
hoursNote: Thu to Mon 10am to 4pm; closed Tue and Wed; adults $15, under 13 free with an adult

name: Le Bons Bay
description:
A wide, gently shelving sandy beach at the end of Le Bons Bay Road, off the Summit Road east of Akaroa. It is about a kilometre across, good for swimming and usually quiet, with a grassy domain behind it that has shady trees, picnic tables and a clean toilet by the car park.

There are no shops, so bring your own food and drink. In summer a coffee and ice cream van is sometimes parked up.
Local tip: The road down is sealed but very narrow and winding, so take it slowly, and think twice before bringing a large campervan.
hoursNote: Open any time; free; toilets and picnic tables; no shops

name: Hinewai Reserve
description:
A 1,250 hectare private reserve where old farmland has been left to grow back into native forest since 1987. The Maurice White Native Forest Trust runs it, and anyone can walk it for free. About 20km of signposted tracks range from 10 minute strolls to half day circuits, with waterfalls, birdsong and big views out to the peninsula's peaks.

The Hinewai Falls loop is about 4.3km and takes 1.5 to 2.5 hours from the car park and visitor centre on Long Bay Road, around 12 minutes' drive from Akaroa. The visitor centre has toilets, drinking water and hand-drawn maps. Dogs, bikes, camping, fires and smoking are all banned.
Local tip: Some tracks are steep and rough, so wear proper shoes, and leave something in the donation box, since the reserve runs on them.
hoursNote: Open any time on foot; free, donations welcome; no dogs, bikes, fires or smoking

name: Akaroa Lighthouse and Garden of Tāne
description:
An easy walk along Beach Road from the village to Akaroa's white wooden lighthouse, built in 1878 to 1879 and first lit on 1 January 1880. It originally stood at the harbour heads, and in 1980 it was cut into three pieces and moved to Cemetery Point. You can look around the outside for free, and on weekend afternoons volunteers open it up for a small fee.

Behind it, the Garden of Tāne is a council reserve with a maze of tracks through big old trees and native bush, several early settler cemeteries and lookouts over the harbour. Allow up to an hour to wander it.
Local tip: Walk out along the waterfront to the lighthouse, climb up through the Garden of Tāne, and come back down Rue Jolie past its main entrance.
hoursNote: Outside and garden open any time; lighthouse interior usually Sat and Sun 1pm to 3pm; dogs on leash in the garden

name: Kaimoana Takeaways
description:
A small fish and chip shop at 120 Rue Jolie, a short walk from the Akaroa waterfront, and one of the best reviewed takeaways in town. Reviewers rate the Chatham Islands blue cod, the light, crispy batter and the generous serves. There are kūmara fries, curly fries and halloumi fritters too, and the pineapple fritters rolled in cinnamon sugar are worth saving room for.

It is takeaway only, with no tables.
Local tip: Carry your order across the road and eat it on the foreshore, looking out over the harbour.

name: Akaroa Harbour Lookout
description:
A roadside pull-off on State Highway 75 as the road drops from Hilltop towards Barrys Bay, giving you the first full view down Akaroa Harbour and across the rim of the old volcanic crater. It is the classic photo on the way in.

It is free, open any time and only needs a few minutes, though locals also rate it for sunset.
Local tip: Stop on the way down to get your bearings. You can pick out Akaroa, Barrys Bay and Duvauchelle from here before you reach them.
hoursNote: Open any time; free; small roadside parking area

name: Little River Rail Trail and Village
description:
A flat, easy to intermediate cycle trail along the old railway line from Christchurch to Little River, 60km in all. The best stretch is the last 23km from the old Motukarara station, which runs past the bird-filled wetlands of Te Waihora/Lake Ellesmere to Little River village.

Little River makes a good stop roughly halfway on the drive to Akaroa, with a popular café and general store, an art gallery and places to stay. The Little River Café and Store is open daily from 7.30am to 4pm.
Local tip: Skip the suburban first sections and start at Motukarara, and take plenty of water and sunscreen, since there is little shade and the sandflies can be bad in summer.
hoursNote: Trail open any time; free; Motukarara to Little River 23 km; café daily 7.30am to 4pm

name: Akaroa Freedom Camping Area
description:
The only designated free camping spot in Akaroa, in the Akaroa Boat Park off Woodills Road at the northern end of town. It has 18 marked spaces on tarseal for certified self-contained vehicles, with a limit of two nights in any 30 day period.

It is really a car park by the water, but the harbour views are good, there are rubbish bins on site and toilets a short walk away, and the village is about five minutes on foot. Tents and vehicles that aren't self-contained are banned from freedom camping anywhere in Akaroa or on Banks Peninsula, and the fine is $400.
Local tip: It fills up by late afternoon in summer, so arrive early or line up a paid campground as a backup.
hoursNote: Certified self-contained only; 18 spaces; max 2 nights in any 30 days; toilets nearby

name: Okains Bay Camping Ground
description:
A big campground behind the beach at Okains Bay, with plenty of grassy unpowered sites, a sheltered lagoon for swimming and kayaking, a playground and very dark skies for stargazing. Sites start from about $30 a night for two adults, and children under 5 stay free.

There are kitchens, toilets, pay showers, a laundry and a dump station, but the water has to be boiled before drinking. Dogs, fires and generators aren't allowed, and you book online with your number plate, which opens the gate.
Local tip: Stay the night and visit the Okains Bay Museum just up the road the next morning, and bring drinking water from home.
hoursNote: Book online; no dogs, fires or generators; boil water before drinking; under 5s free

name: Onuku Farm Hostel
description:
A relaxed backpackers and campground on a working sheep farm on the hill above the harbour at Ōnuku, a short drive south of Akaroa. As well as the hostel there is a campervan and tent area, plus simple "stargazer" huts with see-through roofs at about $50 a night, with sleeping bags for hire.

Reviewers like the views, the clean showers and shared kitchen, the animals wandering around and the walks on the farm. The hostel also runs dolphin swimming trips. It is open from October to the end of April.
Local tip: The access road is steep and single lane, so take it slowly, and pack light, since some huts and campsites are a walk from the car park.
hoursNote: Open October to end of April; closed in winter
